children: India is emerging as a beneficiary of investors’ shift away from artificial intelligence stocks, while easing tensions over Iran could support a broader rally in markets outside the United States, according to Christopher Wood, strategist at Jefferies.

In his "Greed & Fear" report dated November 12, Wood said doubts about returns on AI spending were encouraging portfolio managers to seek other investments. He highlighted India’s economic recovery and signs of stronger private investment, alongside renewed foreign buying.
However, he identified a fresh escalation involving Iran as the biggest risk to Indian equities. He retained energy stocks in his portfolios as protection against renewed geopolitical tensions.
Foreign investors return to India

Foreign investors bought a net $7.2 billion of Indian equities over the three weeks covered by the report. This included a record weekly purchase of $5.2 billion in the week ended November 6, according to figures cited by Wood.
The buying followed net foreign sales of $32.4 billion since the start of 2026 and $51.2 billion since the start of 2025.
Wood said Indian valuations remained comparatively modest against historical levels. The Nifty traded at 18.4 times one-year forward earnings, while the Nifty MidCap 100 traded at 23.1 times.

He also pointed to machinery imports as evidence that a long-awaited private sector investment cycle was taking hold. Imports rose from $29 billion in the financial year ended March 2021 to $62 billion in the year ended March 2026. They reached $67 billion over the 12 months to September.
Domestic equity mutual fund inflows continued to support the market. These totalled 350 billion rupees in October and 3.9 trillion rupees over the first 10 months of 2026, according to the report.
However, rising share supply had restrained benchmark indices. Monthly equity supply reached $9.2 billion in September and $6.6 billion in October, compared with $1 billion in April.
Falling returns challenge AI spending
Wood maintained his view that the AI capital spending cycle may have peaked, despite forecasts for further growth next year.

He cited Jefferies research showing that the consensus forecast for median 2027 return on invested capital among four major U.S. cloud companies had fallen to 16.8% from 21.7% at the start of the year.

image.alt: The consensus forecast for median 2027 return on invested capital among four major U.S. cloud companies fell to 16.8% from 21.7% at the start of the year.

children: The analysis covered Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet and Amazon. Their aggregate capital spending as a share of sales was forecast to rise from 11.4% in 2023 to 44.2% in 2027.

Wood said stronger pricing power for large language models could revive momentum in AI stocks. Without that evidence, he expected investors to focus increasingly on identifying successful AI applications.
The shift was already visible in U.S. pharmaceuticals. The Dow Jones U.S. Pharmaceuticals Index had outperformed the Solactive U.S. AI & Big Data Index by 31% since early October, the report said.
Iran tensions remain central to outlook
Wood said Brent crude’s
21% decline from its October 30 peak of $118 a barrel suggested growing confidence that US President Donald Trump would avoid further escalation with Iran.
A resolution without further violence could renew the outperformance of non-US equities, he said. Europe could benefit particularly from lower energy prices.
According to the report, MSCI Europe had underperformed MSCI USA by 11% since the conflict began at the end of February. It had since outperformed by 7.2% from October 8.
Wood nevertheless described the prospect of avoiding renewed escalation as a close call, putting the odds at roughly 55 to 45.
He said he would maintain energy holdings across his portfolios and viewed the recent decline in energy shares as a buying opportunity for investors seeking protection against renewed tensions.
China offers a contrarian opportunity
Wood also identified China as a potential destination for investors seeking alternatives to AI, while acknowledging continued weakness in domestic economic data.
MSCI China

traded at 9.3 times 12-month forward earnings, according to the report. Wood pointed to renewed buying through exchange-traded funds associated with state-backed investors as a possible source of support.
Nine mainland equity index ETFs known to be actively traded by China’s “national team” recorded net inflows of 156 billion yuan in the week ended November 6, the report said, citing Bloomberg data.
Wood also announced changes to his China long-only equity portfolio. He introduced ACM Research
and hotel operator Atour Lifestyle
at weights of 4% each, replacing Tencent Music
and China Communications Services
He increased Zijin Gold International’s
allocation by one percentage point in both the China and Asia ex-Japan long-only portfolios, funded by reductions in Zijin Mining

title: India stands to gain as investors look beyond AI, Jefferies’ Wood says
